demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

vignette:
Michael Varela had spent most of his adult life in the woods outside Missoula, marking timber, checking stands after storms, and trusting his judgment in places where one wrong step could mean a twisted ankle or a felled branch. At 54, married, and usually steady in the routines of field work, he came to therapy carrying a single event that had split his life in two. Two years earlier, while supervising a thinning operation on a steep slope, he had signaled to a younger crewman to move back just as a cut log shifted unexpectedly. Michael had thought the path was clear; instead, the log struck the man's leg and drove him hard into the ground. Michael remembered the man's shout, the jagged angle of the limb, and the awful stillness afterward while he waited for help. The injury was serious, and though the crewman survived, Michael had been left with a sense that one small error from him had set the whole thing in motion.

In the weeks after the accident, Michael found that reminders could arrive through his body before they came through his mind. A twinge of pain in his own leg, a stiff back after carrying equipment, or even the pressure of his boots on uneven ground would pull him back to that slope, and with the sensation came the image of the injured man on the forest floor. When those reminders hit, he felt his body lock into the same position he had been in at the moment of the accident, as if he were once again braced on the hillside, frozen between giving the wrong signal and watching the harm unfold. Even now, a glimpse of the man's face in the company yard or passing close by another worker on a trail could do the same. The memories brought not only the body sensation but an immediate surge of grief for what had been done to the other man and rage at himself for failing to prevent it, and those feelings quickly hardened into the belief that there was something about him that had made the event happen. He began to tell himself that he could no longer rely on himself, that the instincts that had once made him good at the job had betrayed him, and that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him for decades.

That conviction fed into a constant state of watchfulness that took over both his work and home life. Michael found himself unable to relax even in his own living room, and when strangers approached him in ordinary situations-a man coming up the aisle in a store, a neighbor crossing too quickly in a parking lot-he felt threatened before anyone had said a word. He watched people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning posture, tone, and distance with a vigilance that left him tense and exhausted. In the woods, he became especially alert to anyone walking near him on a trail or stepping too close at the worksite, and he began choosing routes that let him keep other people farther away. That constant threat-monitoring made the memories come more easily: the more he braced for danger, the more his mind returned to the accident, and each return seemed to confirm his fear that he was unsafe and unfit. It also pulled his attention toward the very cues that set him off. Pain in his body, the sight of someone injured, the physical proximity of another person on a narrow path-each of these now felt charged, and the more he scanned for danger, the more those reminders stood out to him as proof that the event still had power over his life.

Over months, Michael's world narrowed around these reactions. He avoided lingering near the injured crewman at the yard and found reasons to stay back when conversations turned to accidents or injuries. He stopped volunteering for tasks that put him close to other workers on steep ground, and his marriage had become strained by the way he stayed keyed up and unreachable even at home. What finally brought him in was his fear that one day the tension and self-doubt would cost him his job or make him miss something important again. He hoped for relief from the constant scanning and the body memories, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he really had become the kind of man who could not trust himself around others, or trust himself at all.
